subject: Psychiatry
subtopic: Selective mutism and separation anxiety disorder
vignette: A 4-year-old girl speaks normally and fluently at home with her family but has not spoken a word at preschool for the past 3 months. She communicates by pointing and nodding at school and appears anxious in that setting. Her speech and language development are otherwise normal, and she has no neurologic deficits. Her teachers are concerned about her social interactions.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Separation anxiety disorder with factitious physical complaints to avoid school
Autism spectrum disorder with impaired language development
Intellectual disability with delayed speech and language
Social anxiety disorder with generalized fear of all social situations
Selective mutism with refraining from speech in certain situations

explanation_correct: Selective mutism has onset before age 5 and involves refraining from speech in certain situations despite speaking in other, more comfortable situations, lasting at least 1 month. Development of speech and language is not typically impaired, as in this girl who speaks normally at home. It commonly coexists with social anxiety disorder and interferes with social and academic functioning. Treatment includes behavioral, family, and play therapy and SSRIs.

explanation_incorrect.A: Separation anxiety disorder involves overwhelming fear of separation from attachment figures and may cause factitious complaints to avoid school, not selective refusal to speak in specific settings.
explanation_incorrect.B: Autism spectrum disorder involves social/communication deficits and restricted behaviors, and speech/language development is typically impaired, which is not the case here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Intellectual disability involves global cognitive deficits and adaptive impairment; this girl's language development and cognition are normal.
explanation_incorrect.D: Social anxiety disorder is a broader exaggerated fear of embarrassment in many social situations; this girl's deficit is specific to speaking, consistent with selective mutism, though the two often coexist.

educationalObjective: Selective mutism is onset before age 5 with refusal to speak in specific situations for at least 1 month despite normal speech elsewhere and normal language development.

subject: Psychiatry
subtopic: Selective mutism and separation anxiety disorder
vignette: A 7-year-old boy has episodes of intense distress each morning before school, with stomachaches and headaches that improve once he is allowed to stay home. He repeatedly expresses fear that something terrible will happen to his mother while he is away. Physical examination and laboratory evaluation are normal. Symptoms have persisted for 7 weeks and significantly impair his attendance.
question: Which of the following best explains the cause and appropriate treatment of this child's somatic complaints?

options.text: Factitious disorder imposed on another; parents should be reported to child protective services
Separation anxiety disorder with factitious complaints to avoid school; treat with CBT, play therapy, and family therapy
Somatic symptom disorder; management with regular visits and reassurance only
Generalized anxiety disorder; treatment with SSRIs and benzodiazepines
Selective mutism; treatment with behavioral therapy and SSRIs

explanation_correct: Separation anxiety disorder is an overwhelming fear of separation from home or an attachment figure lasting at least 4 weeks. It can lead to factitious physical complaints to avoid school, as in this boy whose symptoms remit when he stays home. Although this level of fear can be normal up to age 3-4, it is pathological at age 7. Treatment includes CBT, play therapy, and family therapy.

explanation_incorrect.A: Factitious disorder imposed on another involves a caregiver intentionally causing or fabricating illness in the child; here the child's complaints arise from his own anxiety about separation.
explanation_incorrect.C: Somatic symptom disorder involves multiple bodily complaints with excessive thoughts and anxiety about symptoms for months to years, not the school-avoidance pattern driven by separation fears.
explanation_incorrect.D: Generalized anxiety disorder involves excessive worry about multiple areas of life for most days over at least 6 months, not fear specifically about separation from an attachment figure.
explanation_incorrect.E: Selective mutism involves refraining from speech in certain situations despite speaking elsewhere; this child's primary problem is separation distress with somatic complaints.

educationalObjective: Separation anxiety disorder (fear of separation ≥4 weeks) can cause factitious school-avoidance complaints; treat with CBT, play therapy, and family therapy.

subject: Psychiatry
subtopic: Selective mutism and separation anxiety disorder
vignette: The parents of a 2-year-old ask whether their child's distress when left with a babysitter is normal. The child becomes upset at separation but is easily comforted and settles quickly, with no difficulty sleeping or attending daycare. Development is appropriate for age. The parents are reassured that this behavior is a normal part of development.
question: Up to what age is such separation distress considered normal behavior rather than separation anxiety disorder?

options.text: Separation distress is never normal at any age

explanation_correct: Separation anxiety — overwhelming fear of separation from home or an attachment figure — can be normal behavior up to age 3-4. Separation anxiety disorder is diagnosed when the fear is excessive, lasts at least 4 weeks, and causes significant impairment. This toddler's easily comforted, brief distress with normal functioning is a normal developmental phenomenon.

explanation_incorrect.B: By ages 7-8, persistent overwhelming separation fear causing impairment would meet criteria for separation anxiety disorder rather than being considered normal.
explanation_incorrect.C: At ages 10-12, significant separation distress with impairment is pathological and warrants evaluation for separation anxiety disorder.
explanation_incorrect.D: Separation distress persisting into adolescence with impairment is not a normal developmental expectation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Separation distress is a normal part of early development up to age 3-4, so it is not accurate to say it is never normal.

educationalObjective: Separation fear is a normal developmental behavior up to age 3-4; beyond this, persistent fear lasting at least 4 weeks with impairment suggests separation anxiety disorder.
